title: Retrieval questions teach, not just measure
statement: Use low-stakes retrieval questions as learning events, not only as measures, because practising recall beats restudying.
example: In one meta-analysis, practice testing beat restudying at g = +0.51.
detail: An assessment BrainLift in the reading course's feedback treats multiple-choice questions as learning events first and puts the testing effect for multiple-choice practice at g = +0.70 against restudying; its own notes on the meta-analysis behind the figure give g = +0.51 for practice testing against restudying, g = +0.93 against no activity, and g = +0.70 for multiple-choice practice tests against g = +0.48 for short-answer ones. The course's evaluation criteria make active recall the primary learning event, not passive consumption (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/timeback-course-eval/references/eval-criteria.md`, line 38).
against: The same BrainLift warns that plausible wrong options can implant false knowledge when no feedback follows, a risk that feedback largely removes (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback3/WF - Assessment  Feedback Brain - 260624-200115.md`, line 1991).

evidence.quote: The testing effect for MCQ-based practice (g = +0.70 vs. restudying) is one of the largest effect sizes in educational psychology.
Practice testing produced moderate effect sizes vs. restudying (g = +0.51) and large effect sizes vs. no activity (g = +0.93).
MC practice tests showed a larger effect size (g = +0.70) than short-answer tests (g = +0.48)
Active recall is the primary learning event, not passive consumption.
Key words: study a set, then recall each word into a gap. Each word comes back in a sentence about the text with a … blank where it goes, cued by its meaning, and the student types it from memory.
Study each word and what it means. Then put them away, and put each back into its sentence from memory.
